total Gap #

Upper bounds — holds for every total

  • \(\mathrm{I}^{1}(p) = O(\deg(p)^2) \text{ for bounded } p:\{-1,1\}^n\to[-1,1]\)
    FHKL16
    Improves the $O(d^3)$ of [BackursBavarian14]. For homogeneous $p$ the bound is $O(d\log d)$.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\exists \text{ bounded } p:\ \mathrm{I}^{1}(p) = \Omega(\deg(p)\log\deg(p))\)·
    FHKL16
    Matching the homogeneous upper bound; the truth for general bounded $p$ is between $d\log d$ and $d^2$.

Why this is a query statement: if a quantum algorithm makes $T$ queries then its acceptance probability is a bounded polynomial of degree $\le 2T$, so $L_1$-influence bounds for bounded polynomials transfer directly to quantum query algorithms.

see also: \(\mathrm{I}^{1}(f)\), \(\deg(f)\), \(\mathrm{Q}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\) data/relations/05-fourier.yaml

facts: Improved to $O(\deg(p)^2)$ in general and $O(d\log d)$ for homogeneous $p$ [FHKL16], with a matching example for monotone functions.
A quantum algorithm making $T$ queries has acceptance probability $p$ with $\deg(p)\le 2T$, so these bounds transfer directly to query complexity.

The Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture is proved: bounded degree-$d$ polynomials have $\max_i\mathrm{Inf}_i(p)\ge c\,\mathrm{Var}(p)^{5/2}/d^6$ [PSI26AaronsonAmbainis, Turturean26]. This gives classical simulation of quantum query algorithms on most uniformly random inputs. Cleaner expositions: [BDST26AA] and [HMP26AA].
